column1: # Well-known system account names, so /etc/passwd findings can say what an account is for
# instead of just "system account". Not exhaustive and not a security boundary - it only
# improves the labels. A system account NOT in here is fine; it is the ones with a login
# shell, UID 0, or a password that the detector actually flags.

column3: UID 0, the administrator account. Its shell is expected to be interactive.
Generic unprivileged account for daemons that do not need their own user.
Historical owner of system binaries. No login.
Its shell is /bin/sync, which just flushes disks and logs out - not a real login.
Owns game score files. No login.
Owns cached manual pages. No login.
The account Apache/nginx workers run as on Debian/Ubuntu. A web shell runs as this user.
The account the web server runs as on Arch.
UID 65534, the account with (almost) no rights. Used to drop privilege.
The unprivileged account sshd drops to for network-facing code. It must have no shell.
PostgreSQL's account. Owns the database cluster; often has a real shell for admin use.
Often a real login account used for git-over-ssh (gitosis/gitolite). A shell here can be intentional.
